newsitem.title: FRANCE: Uganda seeks faster debt relief-minister.
newsitem.headline: Uganda seeks faster debt relief-minister.

text.p: Uganda called on Friday for fast progress in a debt-relief initiative for poor countries under which it hopes to be an early beneficiary.

In Paris for talks with donor nations at the World Bank, Finance Minister J Mayanja-Nkangi said he was disappointed negotiations on implementing the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) initiative were not moving faster.
"Of course," he said when asked if he were disappointed at the pace of the talks. "We would have wished to have this debt relief yesterday."
Works, Transport and Communications Minister John Nasasira echoed Mayanja-Nkangi. "The ball is not in our court. We would like to have the debt relief move faster," Nasasira said.

Uganda is likely to be one of the first countries to benefit from HIPC, a debt exit initiative launched by the International Monetary Fund and World Bank and supported by the Paris Club of creditor nations.
HIPC is meant to enable poor countries with heavy debt and good policy performance to escape from unsustainable debt and focus on development, the World Bank said.

Uganda said it was pleased with the level of aid pledged for the 1997 tax year. Donor nations promised about $750 million in project and technical assistance and programme support at a meeting on Thursday and Friday.
The pledge also includes $50 million for debt servicing.
"We are satisfied with the aid," Nasasira said.
World Bank officials said the first countries to benefit from HIPC would probably see implementation in the spring and that Uganda had a good chance of being at the front of the pack.
"Under all the criteria Uganda qualifies," said James Adams, the World Bank's country director for Uganda. "Right from the beginning, Uganda has been viewed as eligible."
Mayanja-Nkangi said he hoped Uganda, which has already been given a 67 percent debt write-off by the Paris Club, would eventually be able to benefit from better terms.
"I want the whole thing written off," he said. "One hundred percent."
The Paris Club agreed in September that it could write off up to 80 percent of the stock of debt of poor countries on a case-by-case basis.
Uganda has foreign debt of $3.3 billion, of which 75 percent is owed to multilateral institutions, mostly to the World Bank, and 21 percent is bilateral debt.
Of its bilateral debt, only 10 percent is owed to Paris Club members and 11 percent is owed to non-Paris Club members.
